title: Consider the lilies (Luke 12:22–34)
hook: the ravens don't sow, the lilies don't spin

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farmer built bigger barns and didn't get one evening to enjoy them. Your line was this night.

Two in the morning, and the ceiling has become very interesting. Rent, a test result, a child who hasn't texted back, the thing said at work that can't be unsaid. Worry doesn't keep office hours. Right after the rich man and his barns, Jesus turns to his disciples, people who have no barns at all, and talks about exactly this. He doesn't give them a budget. He tells them to look at two things: a bird and a flower.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `WORRY KEEPS NO OFFICE HOURS.` → `A BIRD AND A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Jesus says: be not solicitous for your life, what you'll eat, or for your body, what you'll wear. Solicitous is the Douay's word for anxious. The first picture: "Consider the ravens, for they sow not, neither do they reap, neither have they storehouse nor barn, and God feedeth them." No barn: a pointed word after yesterday. Luke says ravens, where Matthew says the birds of the air. The raven was a noisy black scavenger, and the Law of Moses listed it among the birds not to be eaten. God feeds it anyway. The second picture: "Consider the lilies, how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin." Spinning thread was daily work, the way people made cloth. The lilies make nothing, yet Solomon in all his glory wasn't dressed like one of them. Which flower did Jesus mean? Nobody knows for sure; readers have guessed anemones, irises and others. Then: which of you, by taking thought, can add to his stature one cubit? Worry adds nothing. And a tender line: fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you a kingdom. So sell what you have, give alms, make purses that don't wear out, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Consider means look closely, take your time. Jesus doesn't argue people out of worry. He asks them to look at something alive and let it teach them.
screen: `BE NOT SOLICITOUS: DON'T BE ANXIOUS.` · `RAVENS: NO STOREHOUSE, NO BARN.` · `LILIES: THEY NEITHER LABOR NOR SPIN.` · `FEAR NOT, LITTLE FLOCK.` · then, large: `CONSIDER THE LILIES, HOW THEY GROW.`

segments.voice: If you can, find a real flower, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, or a picture if that's all you have, and consider it slowly: the color at the center, the folds of the petals, how it's simply being what it is. When a worry walks in, notice it and bring your eyes back to the flower. If you pray, let it remind you who clothes it.
Lilies. Jesus' cure for anxiety: look closely at ravens with no barns and flowers that never spin, and remember who feeds and clothes them. Today's word.
Your line: fear not, little flock. Ravens and lilies, both cared for. Four hundred sixty-four days now.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this teaching on anxiety in the Gospel readings at Mass, and some pray with it when they speak of trusting God's providence, his care for all he has made.

original.note: Greek: consider the lilies. The verb means look closely, take it in, study it.

trapdoor: what you thought: consider the lilies means don't plan anything.
what it means: Jesus asks anxious people to look closely at God's care for ravens and flowers, and to set their hearts on the kingdom.
what a scholar hears: Luke says ravens (korakas), birds the Law listed as unclean (Leviticus 11:15), where Matthew says birds of the air.

chat.says: Is Jesus saying I shouldn't plan or work at all, like the lilies?
options: No, he's saying worry adds nothing; look at what God feeds and clothes, and trust.
Yes, he wanted his followers to stop working and simply wait for food.
No, he's saying flowers are holier than people because they never toil.
chat.meaning: Jesus asks people to consider ravens and lilies: worry can't add a cubit, and the Father who feeds and clothes them cares for his little flock.

Solomon.meaning: a king of Israel, famous for his glory

anemones.meaning: wildflowers, one guess for Jesus' lilies
